why: The verdict is deliberately not 'keep-ours'. Every SCANNING and SIGNING capability in this space is better done by software that already exists, and verify.py does not reimplement any of it: SCANNERS is a five-entry dispatch table that shells out to osv-scanner, trivy, grype, cargo-audit and pip-audit, and sign-check shells out to `gh attestation verify` or `cosign verify-blob`. What is kept is the roughly 120 lines that none of them provide: a per-ARTIFACT decision record with a refusal rule attached (evaluate(), the four properties, the non-waivable hash), keyed on the sha256 of bytes that landed on this machine rather than on a package name in a manifest. Every alternative below is scoped to a PROJECT'S DECLARED DEPENDENCIES -- a Cargo.lock, a requirements.txt, an image manifest -- and the driving case is not a dependency at all: a release zip and an install script downloaded by a human at a terminal. cargo-vet is the nearest neighbour philosophically and is the model this was shaped after; it is rejected on scope, not on quality. The second kept property is that ABSENCE IS RECORDED: on this machine, measured 2026-07-30, none of the five scanners and neither cosign nor syft is installed, so any design that assumed a scanner would report clean on a machine where nothing ran. `unavailable` aggregating to a refusal is the rule the repo already runs on (gate.py: UNCOVERED fails) applied one layer out.

alternatives.name: cargo-vet (Mozilla, github.com/mozilla/cargo-vet, fetched 2026-07-30)
alternatives.covers: The closest match in intent, and the design this borrowed from: a tool 'to help projects ensure that third-party Rust dependencies have been audited by a trusted entity', with a supply-chain/ directory of audit records and importable audits from other organisations. Audit-record-with-a-verdict is exactly the shape of state/supply-chain.jsonl, and its imported-audits model is strictly better than anything here because trust composes across organisations.
alternatives.gap: Scope. It governs crates.io dependencies of a Cargo project. It has no way to express 'this zip came from this GitHub release, hashed to X, and a human accepted it on this date', which is the driving case. This repo also builds no Rust crate of its own; the operator is Rust-first in other repositories.
alternatives.cost: cargo install, plus a supply-chain/ directory and an ongoing audit obligation per dependency.
alternatives.maturity: Mozilla-maintained, book at mozilla.github.io/cargo-vet. I fetched the repo page only; I did NOT read the book, did NOT install it, and did NOT verify its current release cadence.

alternatives.name: cargo-deny (Embark Studios, github.com/EmbarkStudios/cargo-deny, fetched 2026-07-30)
alternatives.covers: Four checks: advisories, bans, licenses, and SOURCES, the last being 'ensures crates only come from sources you trust', which is the only provenance-shaped check found in any alternative here. Version 0.19.9 at fetch, dual MIT/Apache-2.0, MSRV 1.88.0, ships a GitHub Action.
alternatives.gap: Same scope wall as cargo-vet, and its source check is about registry/git origins declared in a manifest, not about bytes on disk. Nothing in it produces a per-artifact record.
alternatives.cost: cargo install plus a deny.toml. Recommended separately for any Rust crate this ecosystem builds; that recommendation is not in conflict with keeping this component.
alternatives.maturity: 2.4k stars, 79 open issues, actively released. Not installed, not run.

alternatives.name: Trivy (Aqua Security, github.com/aquasecurity/trivy, fetched 2026-07-30)
alternatives.covers: Apache-2.0, 37.1k stars. Scans container images, filesystems, remote git repos, VM images and Kubernetes clusters for OS-package and dependency CVEs, IaC misconfiguration, secrets and licences. The broadest single scanner in this list and the one most likely to be the right first install.
alternatives.gap: Answers 'what is wrong with these bytes', never 'where did these bytes come from and who decided to keep them'. It emits findings, not a decision. ADOPTED as a scan backend rather than rejected.
alternatives.cost: A Go binary install. Not present on this machine at review time.
alternatives.maturity: Widely adopted across Docker, Kubernetes and CI platforms per its own README. I did NOT run it, and did NOT verify the exact current release number, which the fetched page renders as a badge rather than text.

alternatives.name: OSV-Scanner (Google, github.com/google/osv-scanner, fetched 2026-07-30)
alternatives.covers: Apache-2.0, Go. Matches dependencies against the OSV database across npm, pip, Maven, Go modules and Cargo, with call analysis 'to determine if a vulnerable function is actually being used', plus container scanning, licence checking, offline scanning and guided remediation. Tried first by verify.py because call analysis makes it the least noisy on source trees.
alternatives.gap: Advisory matching over a dependency graph. Nothing about artifact provenance. ADOPTED as a scan backend.
alternatives.maturity: V2 referenced as beta on the fetched page. Not run; exact version not verified.

alternatives.name: Grype + Syft (Anchore, github.com/anchore/grype, fetched 2026-07-30)
alternatives.covers: Apache-2.0. Vulnerability scanning of container images, filesystems and Syft-produced SBOMs. The SBOM pairing is the real differentiator: Syft produces the inventory, Grype matches it.
alternatives.gap: Same as Trivy, and weaker for the driving case specifically, because a downloaded release binary arrives with no SBOM and generating one for a stripped binary is the weakest input Syft takes. ADOPTED as a scan backend, third in preference order.
alternatives.cost: Two Go binaries. Both absent here.
alternatives.maturity: Anchore-sponsored, actively maintained. The fetched page does not state a version in text. Not run.

alternatives.name: cargo-audit (RustSec, github.com/rustsec/rustsec, fetched 2026-07-30)
alternatives.covers: One of six crates in the RustSec repo alongside cargo-lock, cvss, platforms, rustsec and rustsec-admin. Audits Cargo.lock against the RustSec advisory database. The correct tool for the Rust side and the operator is Rust-first.
alternatives.gap: Reads a lockfile. Silent about a downloaded binary. ADOPTED as a scan backend.
alternatives.cost: cargo install cargo-audit. cargo is present on this machine; cargo-audit is not.
alternatives.maturity: The canonical Rust advisory tool. Not run this session.

alternatives.name: pip-audit (PyPA with Trail of Bits, github.com/pypa/pip-audit, fetched 2026-07-30)
alternatives.covers: Apache-2.0, PyPA-maintained with Trail of Bits and Google support, requires Python 3.10+. Audits environments and requirements files against the Python Packaging Advisory Database via the PyPI JSON API, and can also query OSV and ESMS. Emits columnar, JSON, CycloneDX or Markdown.
alternatives.gap: Scope again, and nearly irrelevant to this repo's own code, which is stdlib-only by design and has no requirements.txt outside intent-control-plane. ADOPTED as a scan backend for artifacts that bring Python dependencies with them.
alternatives.cost: A pip install into some environment. Absent here.

alternatives.name: sigstore/cosign (github.com/sigstore/cosign, fetched 2026-07-30) and SLSA provenance (slsa.dev/spec/v1.0/levels, fetched 2026-07-30)
alternatives.covers: cosign is Apache-2.0, 2.x stable, described by its own README as receiving periodic updates with future work moving to sigstore-go. `cosign verify-blob` is precisely the artifact-signature check this component wants, and `cosign verify` covers OCI images. SLSA supplies the vocabulary: Build L1 is provenance exists and may be unsigned, L2 adds a hosted build platform and signed provenance, L3 adds isolation between runs and signing keys inaccessible to user-defined build steps.
alternatives.gap: cosign answers exactly one of the four properties and records nothing; a verification that leaves no row is a verification nobody can cite next month. SLSA is a PRODUCER-side standard: this repo consumes artifacts and cannot make a vendor reach L2, so it is used as vocabulary for what a signature status means rather than as a requirement. cosign is ADOPTED as the second signature backend.
alternatives.cost: A Go binary install. Absent on this machine, which is why gh attestation is tried first.
alternatives.maturity: Sigstore is the mainstream answer for artifact signing. I did NOT run cosign and did NOT verify the current 2.x point release; the fetched README references v2.4.1 in a Dockerfile example, which is an example, not a release statement.

alternatives.name: gh attestation verify (GitHub CLI artifact attestations, docs.github.com, fetched 2026-07-30)
alternatives.covers: Verifies a downloaded artifact binary against a Sigstore bundle: `gh attestation verify PATH -R owner/repo --bundle F --custom-trusted-root trusted_root.jsonl`, with an offline path via `gh attestation download` and `gh attestation trusted-root`. DECISIVE PRACTICAL FACT: gh is the only cryptographic verifier already present on this machine, measured 2026-07-30, so this is the first backend verify.py tries.
alternatives.gap: Only covers artifacts built and attested in GitHub Actions. Says nothing about a vendor-hosted installer at an arbitrary domain, which is the Oak case. Records nothing.
alternatives.maturity: First-party GitHub. I fetched the offline-verification doc page; I did NOT execute a verification, because no attested artifact is recorded in the ledger yet. That is the single largest unverified claim in this record.

alternatives.name: JFrog Artifactory + Xray, and Sonatype Nexus Lifecycle
alternatives.covers: The commercial baseline the operator named: a hosted binary repository plus a policy engine over it, with provenance, licence policy, and CVE gating in one product.
alternatives.gap: Per-seat commercial licensing and a hosted service, for a single-operator harness that publishes no artifacts and proxies no registry. The proxying model also does not fit: the driving artifacts are a GitHub release zip and a vendor installer script, neither of which arrives through a package registry.
alternatives.cost: Licence plus a server. Disproportionate by a very wide margin at this scale.
alternatives.maturity: Mature and not in question. I did NOT check current pricing or whether a free self-hosted OSS tier would cover this use, and that is the honest re-open condition for this row.

alternatives.name: Do nothing: keep refusing unverifiable installs case by case
alternatives.covers: The status quo on 2026-07-30. Costs no code and no install.
alternatives.gap: It is what produced the inconsistency that motivated the component. RTK allowed, Oak refused, nothing written down that would make the next answer predictable, and the operator's argument stands: refusing everything unverifiable does not make the harness safe, it makes it stale.

evidence: Read in full before writing: quality-contract.json (all 82 lines, the 12 declared domains and how a domain is expressed as cmd, builtin, artifact, na_reason or waived); tools/gate/gate.py lines 1-1166 of 1386 (the domain evaluation path, run(), tree_fingerprint(), GATE_OUTPUTS and HARNESS_OUTPUTS with their reasoning, the waiver-expiry rule in eval_domain(), the extra-domain handling in cmd_run() that makes a supply_chain domain readable at all, and cmd_selftest as the convention to copy); docs/QUALITY-CONTRACT.md (all 92 lines, in particular the security row at line 26 which is what established that no existing domain covers provenance, and the prior-art field list at lines 53-70); tools/map/codemap.py header and cmd_selftest (the plant-a-defect-per-guarantee convention that tools/supply/verify.py cmd_selftest copies); docs/prior-art/tools-bus.json as the worked example for this file. Ten pages fetched this session, each cited in the row it supports: github.com/aquasecurity/trivy, github.com/google/osv-scanner, github.com/anchore/grype, github.com/sigstore/cosign, github.com/rustsec/rustsec, github.com/EmbarkStudios/cargo-deny, github.com/mozilla/cargo-vet, github.com/pypa/pip-audit, docs.github.com verify-attestations-offline, slsa.dev/spec/v1.0/levels. Ran locally: `python tools/supply/verify.py selftest` -> 19 checks, all ok, VERDICT every planted defect is caught; `python tools/slop_lint.py docs/adr/0019-supply-chain-verification.md` -> clean. Measured tool presence with `command -v` over eleven binaries: gh, cargo, uv and python present; cosign, trivy, syft, grype, osv-scanner and pip-audit ABSENT. NOT VERIFIED, stated plainly: I installed and ran NONE of the five scanners or cosign, so every claim about their behaviour is from their own documentation and not from execution, and the scan-backend argv lines in SCANNERS are UNEXERCISED -- the flag sets are taken from documentation and no invocation of any of them has ever succeeded on this machine. I did not execute `gh attestation verify` against any real artifact. I did not read the cargo-vet book. I did not check JFrog or Sonatype pricing or free tiers. I did not verify exact current release numbers for Trivy, Grype, OSV-Scanner or cosign, because each project's landing page renders the version as a badge image rather than as text. The ledger is empty, so no end-to-end adopt-a-real-artifact run has ever happened; the selftest exercises evaluate() and the chain, not a real download.
recheck: Any ONE of these re-opens the verdict. (1) `python tools/supply/verify.py status` -- if the ledger is still empty at recheck, this component has never been used on a real artifact and the honest verdict is delete-it, not keep-it. (2) `gh api repos/mozilla/cargo-vet --jq '.pushed_at'` and read mozilla.github.io/cargo-vet for any artifact-level (non-crate) audit record; if cargo-vet grows a way to record an audit of an arbitrary file hash, adopt it and delete evaluate(). (3) `gh api repos/aquasecurity/trivy --jq '.pushed_at'` plus a search for 'trivy provenance attestation record' -- Trivy already reads attestations, and if it gains a persistent per-artifact decision ledger the scan and record halves collapse into one tool. (4) Search 'sigstore-go artifact policy ledger' and re-read github.com/sigstore/cosign: the README states future development moves to sigstore-go, and a library with a decision-record layer would replace both backends and the ledger. (5) Re-run the presence sweep; if three or more scanners are installed by then, the `unavailable` path that this design is built around has stopped being the common case and the refusal rule should be re-tuned.
what_ours_does: 795 lines in one stdlib-only file, of which roughly 200 are the WHY docstring and inline reasoning and roughly 230 are cmd_selftest. The substantive code is small on purpose. append()/read_ledger()/canonical() are a hash-chained append-only JSONL ledger at state/supply-chain.jsonl, same shape as state/bus.jsonl and with the same stated limit: it makes a single edited row visible, it does not defend against a full rewrite with recomputed hashes. evaluate() is the whole decision and is a pure function over ledger rows: it requires a 64-hex sha256 of the installed bytes with no waiver possible, a recorded source, a signature status of 'verified' or a live waiver, and a scan status of 'clean' or 'findings-accepted' or a live waiver; last-write-wins per property, so a re-scan after a fix counts and an old clean verdict cannot be resurrected. Waivers carry a reason and an expiry and an expired one is a refusal rather than a skip, copied verbatim from gate.py's rule. cmd_fetch refuses non-https before writing a byte, deletes the file on an --expect-sha256 mismatch rather than leaving it on disk, and prints an explicit note when no expected hash was supplied because a hash of what arrived and a hash of what the vendor published are different claims. fetch-script is cmd_fetch with execute_forbidden, which is the substitute for `curl | sh`: download, hash, record, refuse to run. cmd_sign_check dispatches to `gh attestation verify` or `cosign verify-blob` and records 'unavailable' with the measured presence of each when neither can run. cmd_scan runs EVERY installed scanner rather than stopping at the first clean one, because two scanners disagreeing is the most useful thing the ledger can hold. cmd_selftest plants 19 defects: no-hash refusal including under a perfect signature and a waiver aimed at it, unscanned and unchecked both refusing, unavailable not passing, the full set adopting, live and expired and undated waivers, findings blocking until accepted, a FAILED signature refusing, most-recent-verdict-wins, chain linkage, an edited row breaking verify-ledger, and a non-https fetch writing nothing.
strongest_counterargument: The ledger is empty and every scanner path is unexercised, so this is 795 lines of process for a decision that has been made twice by hand. The five SCANNERS argv lines have never run: their flags come from documentation, and the first real `verify.py scan` on this machine is as likely to report a usage error as a verdict, at which point the aggregate lands on 'findings' and refuses adoption for the wrong reason. That is a live defect, not a hypothetical, and it is not covered by the selftest because the selftest deliberately touches no subprocess. Second: the four-property rule will be met almost entirely by waivers in practice. Most vendors publish no Sigstore attestation, no scanner is installed here, and the honest path for the next artifact is a signature waiver plus a scan waiver plus a hash, which is one property of evidence and two notes explaining their own absence -- barely more than the checksum check that was already being done by hand for RTK. The counter is that a waiver has an author, a reason and an expiry, and a hand-run sha256sum has none of those, but that is a modest gain for 795 lines. Third and most serious: the residual risk this cannot touch is the one that actually compromises supply chains. xz-utils was signed by its own maintainer, and every check here would have passed it green. This component records where bytes came from and that somebody accepted them. It confers no trust, and the ADR should be re-read by anyone tempted to treat a green adopt row as a safety claim.
